comment_content:
This course covers the fundamentals of economics (basic models like supply–demand, market equilibrium, elasticity, consumer/producer surplus, opportunity cost, and basic policy effects). The material is not conceptually hard, but it becomes “easy” only if you stay consistent. Topics build on each other, so if you fall behind for 1–2 weeks, later chapters feel confusing. Overall, the content is straightforward and very manageable if you spend steady time reviewing and practicing.
Planning tip: After each lecture, spend 30–45 minutes rewriting key graphs/definitions and solving a few short questions. That alone keeps you ahead.

comment_content:
Microeconomics is the branch of economics that focuses on individual agents, such as households and firms, and their interactions in markets. Here’s an overview of the key concepts and topics typically covered in microeconomics:
1. Basic Principles of Microeconomics
Scarcity and Choice: Understanding the fundamental economic problem of limited resources and the necessity of making choices.
Opportunity Cost: The cost of forgoing the next best alternative when making decisions.
2. Supply and Demand
Law of Demand: As prices decrease, quantity demanded increases, and vice versa.
Law of Supply: As prices increase, quantity supplied increases, and vice versa.
Market Equilibrium: The point where supply and demand curves intersect, determining the market price and quantity.
3. Elasticity
Price Elasticity of Demand: Measures how much quantity demanded changes in response to price changes.
Price Elasticity of Supply: Measures how much quantity supplied changes in response to price changes.
Income and Cross Elasticities: Understanding how demand changes with consumer income and prices of related goods.
4. Consumer Behavior
Utility Maximization: The concept of consumers seeking to maximize their satisfaction from goods and services.
Budget Constraints: How consumers allocate their income to various goods and services.
Indifference Curves: Graphical representation of consumer preferences and trade-offs.
5. Production and Costs
Production Functions: The relationship between inputs (labor, capital) and output.
Short-Run vs. Long-Run Costs: Understanding different cost structures and their implications for firms.
Economies of Scale: The cost advantages that firms experience as they increase production.

comment_content: It's quite interesting how relevant macroeconomics is to our lives, allowing us to study the overall functioning of the economy, including how interest rates impact output (GDP), how government policies influence economic conditions, and the relationship between output and price levels through various models. It’s certainly more complex than microeconomics, with many more factors to consider. The course outline begins with Part 1: Introduction to Macroeconomics (Ch. 1-2), which introduces key concepts such as GDP, inflation, and unemployment. Part 2: The Short-Run Closed Economy (IS-LM Model) (Ch. 3-5) explores the goods and financial markets, combining them to construct the IS-LM model and applying it to predict and explain the effects of fiscal and monetary policies, both individually and collectively. These first two parts comprise nearly half of the course, making it crucial to fully understand these concepts as they are foundational for the remainder of the material. Part 3: The Short-Run Open Economy (IS-LM-UIP Model) examines trade, exports, and imports, revisiting concepts from Part 2 while introducing new ideas like real depreciation, interest parity conditions, and flexible versus fixed exchange rates. Part 4: The Medium Run (AS-AD Model) (Ch. 6-7) discusses the labor market and the AS-AD model, integrating it with the IS-LM model, while Part 5: The Long Run (Solow Model) (Ch. 10-12.1) explores the interactions between output and capital, the effects of the savings rate on capital, output, and consumption, as well as the concept of balanced growth. For me, Parts 3 and 5 are the most challenging, while many find Part 4 the hardest; perhaps my lack of DSE economics background makes it easier for me to grasp new concepts that diverge from the DSE syllabus.

comment_content:
This is a common core course for HKUST business school students. In this introductory course to
macroeconomic theory and policy analysis, we will introduce the ways economists look at
economy from an “aggregate” perspective. We will start by introducing key macro variables that
measure aggregate economic performance. The relationship among these key variables will then
be studied under three timeframes: the short run, the medium run, and the long run.
In the short run, we will analyze the goods and financial markets, which form the foundation of
the IS-LM model. A closed economy will be examined first, followed by an open economy in the
short run. We will then move on to the labor market and put all three markets together to derive
the AS-AD model in the medium run. Lastly, if time permits, we will further examine key aspects of
economic growth in the long run. Altogether, the theoretical framework presented in this course
will enable you to predict and analyze the impacts of government fiscal and monetary policies on
the economy. The basic teaching materials closely follow the textbook and lecture notes.
I will use real world examples as much as possible to enhance your understanding of the course
materials. We always hear news and commentaries regarding economic growth, unemployment,
inflation, interest rate, national debt, and financial crisis, etc. Upon completion of this course, you
should be able to understand some of these views and concerns, and to perform your own
analysis in your daily life.

comment_content: This course provides an introduction to macroeconomics. Topics include GDP, inflation, the goods market, the financial market, the IS-LM model, unemployment, the Phillips Curve, exchange rates, economic growth, and the Solow model. I had no prior background in macroeconomics apart from Intro to Microeconomics, so I found the course quite eye-opening. The course focuses more on building intuition and understanding economic relationships than on mathematical derivations. While the models are not explored at a very advanced level, they provide a useful framework for understanding how economies work and how policymakers respond to different situations.
comment_teaching: The instructor has a strong Mainland Chinese accent, so if you are sensitive to this plz think twice. Personally, I thought he was a very good lecturer. His slides contain a lot of information, but what makes the lectures valuable is that he explains the logic behind the models rather than simply reading from the slides. He organizes the material clearly and highlights the key ideas and assumptions behind each model. One thing I particularly appreciated was that he often connected the theories to current economic events and policy discussions. He also introduced some extensions and more advanced ideas beyond the textbook. These additions occasionally appeared in exams and may make the course slightly more challenging than some other sections. However, it was obvious that he genuinely enjoys economics and has a deep understanding of the subject, which made the lectures much more engaging.

Be honest, the workload is heavy. If you expect to work hard only before midterm and final, then you may not get good results.
Attending the lectures is not enough. You should spend extra time per week to review concepts, otherwise you will forget the previous concepts while you are studying new concepts. I will prefer using AI to understand them, AI is a perfect 24-7 learning buddy.
What you should do before midterm and final is NOT understanding concepts, but immerse yourselves into practice questions, in which I will mention in the later part. You should understand the concepts much more early than that.
TAs prepare many self-practice questions. It's nearly impossible to do all of them since it's too much and we still have other courses. If you're not pursuing good grades, you may simply neglect them. If you want to get As, then you should try to read all questions, and understand the answers in case you have no idea on any particular questions (Some questions is not well-designed, you have to identify them and prevent wasting time on them).
Talking about the midterm and final, it is a combination of MCQs and LQs, and more calculation-oriented and diagram-oriented. You need to make sure you understand how to calculate and how to draw diagram in both midterm and final. Well, there is some question like "What is GDP", but the grading is quite lenient, and is not like you must give a formal definition in order to get full mark. To sum up, make sure you understand the calculation and PRACTICE ALL POSSIBLE DRAWINGS of diagram before midterm and final.
My recommendation is: If the ppt shows how to draw the dynamics of, let's say, AS-AD model, under an increase in G, then you can practice to draw the dynamics of AS-AD under a decrease in G and check whether the consequences of all economic variables are opposite to the one on the ppt.
Despite all, it's still better than some MATH and COMP course that is designed to torture students on purpose.
